unCLIP on crash reports: from a narrative to a sketch

The unCLIP recipe behind DALL·E 2 has three steps. First, learn how two kinds of data pair up. Second, learn to redraw one kind from its embedding. Third, learn a bridge from the other kind's embedding. This page runs all three steps on the course crash data, Florida crash reports that have both the officer's narrative and the crash sketch, and reports what worked, what did not, and why.

Every sketch on this page was drawn by the models in this run (64 × 64 pixels). No real crash sketch, narrative or personal detail from the course dataset appears here. If you are enrolled, you can look up any crash ID (for example C0021) in your copy of the dataset.

Can a model draw the crash sketch from the officer's narrative?

A Florida long-form crash report has a typed narrative, in which the officer describes what each vehicle (V1, V2) was doing, and usually a sketch of the scene. In the course dataset, 288 of 350 reports have both. A model that could turn a narrative into a draft sketch would help in two ways: it could draft the missing sketch for a report that has none, and it could flag a report whose narrative and sketch tell different stories. The unCLIP recipe from DALL·E 2 is a natural candidate, because it was built to generate one kind of data (an image) from another (a caption).

The recipe · three models trained one at a time, then chained together for a new crash

The point of the split: only steps 1 and 3 need matched narrative–sketch pairs. Step 2 (the hardest part, drawing) learns from sketches alone. Gray dashed boxes are frozen; green boxes are trained.

The data and the honest split

The split is by corridor: the 38 test crashes come from 2 corridors that none of the models saw during training. A model cannot pass the test by memorizing an intersection's shape or its street names, and that is the situation you face when you deploy on a new road. Validation (43 crashes, 4 other corridors) is used only to pick settings; the test set is scored once at the end.

How a generated sketch is scored

One number per generated sketch · where does the true sketch rank among the 38 test sketches?

ranki = 1 + #{ j : cos(ei, rj) > cos(ei, ri) }
ei
CLIP embedding of the sketch generated for test crash i
rj
CLIP embedding of real test sketch j (j = 1…38)
#{…}
count of the real sketches that look more like the output than the true one does
In words: line up all 38 real test sketches by how much they look like the output, and see where the true one lands. We report the median rank (lower is better) and top-5 (share of crashes whose true sketch lands in the first 5). Guessing gives a median of 19.5 and top-5 of 13%.

Check of the scorer: a real test sketch shifted by 3 pixels ranks its own original first of the time (median rank 1). So the scorer can recognize a sketch; a low score means the output really does not look like the right sketch.

The bottom line, before the details

The recipe runs end to end, and each step can be checked on its own. But narratives that go through all three steps come out as sketches no closer to the right one than chance: median rank 17 to 20.5 of 38, where chance is 19.5.

The weak link is step 1. With 207 training pairs, a narrative picks out its own sketch only a little better than chance (median rank 14). The decoder, given a sketch's own embedding, does redraw something recognizable (median rank 10). Even so, simply looking up the most similar training sketch does better (6.5). The tabs show each step, its training, its results, and three problems we hit along the way.

Step 1 · Learn which narrative goes with which sketch

CLIP learned to pair web photos with their captions. Crash reports are far from that: a narrative runs a median of words ( CLIP tokens, while CLIP reads at most 77), and a sketch is a line drawing with lane lines, vehicle boxes, arrows and small labels. So we first check what CLIP does with no training (zero-shot), then train a small head on the 207 training pairs.

The pairing model · frozen CLIP on both sides, one small trained head on the text side

Why only a head: 207 pairs are far too few to retrain CLIP's 150 million weights, so we keep CLIP and learn a small correction on the narrative side.

L = − (1/N) Σi log [ exp(s · ctxt,i · cimg,i) / Σj exp(s · ctxt,i · cimg,j) ] (plus the same with narratives and sketches swapped)
N
207 training pairs, all in one batch
ctxt,i
embedding of narrative i (after the head)
cimg,j
embedding of sketch j
s
a learned sharpness number (starts at 14.3, capped at 100)
In words: for each narrative, ask a 207-way multiple-choice question, "which of these sketches is mine?" The answer is a softmax over similarities, and the loss is −log of the probability given to the right sketch. This is a multinomial logit model with 207 alternatives, where the utility of each alternative is s × similarity.
Going deeper (optional): why the sketch side is locked and centred

We first trained a head on both sides. It paired about as well as the final model (test median rank 15 vs. 14), but the image head squeezed the sketch embedding into a few directions. A least-squares map from that head's output back to the original CLIP embedding explains of its variation on test sketches (R², below zero). In other words, almost none of the sketch survives, so a decoder in step 2 would have little to redraw from. unCLIP never fine-tuned CLIP's image encoder, for the same reason: the decoder needs an embedding that still describes the whole picture.

Centring matters because raw CLIP embeddings of these sketches all look alike: any two sketches have a median cosine of . Subtracting the training mean removes the "this is a line drawing" part they all share, so the differences between sketches carry more weight. We picked between raw and centred by validation mean rank (14.8 raw vs. 14.2 centred), before looking at the test set.

The training loss keeps falling as the head learns the 207 pairs.

Validation · mean rank of each narrative's own sketch among the 43 validation sketches

The validation rank stops improving early. The model at epoch (best validation rank) is the one used from here on. Later epochs only memorize the training pairs.

Does a narrative find its own sketch? · similarity of each of the 38 test narratives (rows) to each test sketch (columns)

Hover a cell. Gold outline = the true pair (diagonal).

How to read it: each row is one narrative, and brighter means more similar. If pairing worked, the diagonal would be the brightest cell in every row. After training, more rows have a bright diagonal cell, but most rows still have several other sketches that look as similar.

Results

Side test: what in the narrative does the pairing use?

Do plain word counts pair as well as CLIP's text embedding? And could the pairing be leaning on street and business names, which also appear as labels inside many sketches? To find out, we trained the same small linear pairing on four narrative features, five times each with different random starts. The last two rows keep only words that appear in narratives from at least 4, or at least 8, of the 14 training corridors, which drops most place names.

These runs use linear 128-number heads on both sides, a slightly different setup from the step-1 model above, so compare the rows with each other, not with the table above.

Reading: word counts pair about as well as CLIP text. Removing corridor-specific words makes pairing a little worse (median 11.8 → 13.8), so place names may help somewhat. But the five seeds of the last row range from 10 to 19, so that difference is within the noise.

Evaluation close

Baseline
Chance (median rank 19.5, top-5 13%) and zero-shot CLIP (median 18.5, top-5 15.8%). Zero-shot CLIP is barely better than guessing on crash reports.
Split and why it is honest
By corridor: the 38 test crashes come from 2 corridors no model saw, so memorized street names and intersection shapes cannot help. Settings (epoch, centring) were picked on validation only.
Ugly cases
38 test crashes is a small set: one crash moves top-5 by 2.6 points. Validation and test disagree on which variant is best. The test set has only 2 corridors, so a check "within the same corridor" is not possible.

Step 2 · Learn to redraw a sketch from its embedding

The decoder never sees a narrative. Each training sketch gives its own example: the sketch x and its embedding cimg from the frozen image encoder. This is why unCLIP can train its decoder on far more data than it has captions. Here that means every sketch outside the test set: sketches, shrunk to 64 × 64 pixels (ink = +1, paper = −1).

The decoder · a small U-Net that guesses the static, with two doors for cimg

Two doors, as in unCLIP: door 1 tells every block "which sketch" through a per-channel scale and shift; door 2 lets the attention layers look the embedding up directly. The 64 × 64 and 32 × 32 levels use only door 1, and attention runs at 16 × 16, 8 × 8 and the middle.

zt = √ᾱt · x + √(1 − ᾱt) · ε,    L = ‖ ε − g(zt, w, t, cimg) ‖²
x
a training sketch, 64 × 64 pixels (ink +1, paper −1)
ε
static: random normal numbers, one per pixel
t, ᾱt
step 1…1000 and how much of the sketch survives at that step (1 at the start, near 0 at step 1000; cosine schedule)
g, w
the U-Net and its weights
cimg
this sketch's own embedding from step 1
In words: bury the sketch under a random amount of static, tell the U-Net which sketch it was (through cimg), and ask it to say exactly what static was added. The training signal comes from the sketch itself, so no labels are needed. To generate, start from pure static and remove the guessed static 50 times (DDIM sampling).
SettingValue
Weights (channels 32 / 64 / 64 / 128 at 64 / 32 / 16 / 8 pixels, one residual block per level each way)
Training sketches (all non-test sketches minus drawn on aerial photos; see below). No flips or rotations: a flip turns a left turn into a right turn. Only shifts of up to 3 pixels.
Training steps, batch 16, AdamW at 2 × 10⁻⁴, moving average of the weights (EMA 0.999), minutes on 2 CPU cores
Generating50 DDIM steps from pure static, guidance λ = 2 (see "Going deeper")

Training loss · three versions of the decoder, average over 500 steps

A falling loss does not prove the decoder uses cimg. Version 1's loss falls almost as well as version 3's, yet it ignored the embedding, as the next figure shows. The loss rewards guessing the static, and much of the static can be guessed from the noisy sketch alone.

Three versions, two problems worth knowing

Problem 1 · The first decoder ignored the embedding

In version 1, cimg went in at length 1. Spread over 512 numbers, that is about 0.04 per number, while the step-t signal it is added to is much larger. The embedding entered the network about × weaker than the step signal (size of the added signal: vs. ), and the U-Net learned to work without it. The test: generate twice from the same random static, once with the sketch's embedding and once with "no embedding". If the two pictures are nearly the same, the embedding is not doing anything.

Version 2 multiplies cimg by √512 so each number has about unit size. Version 3 also removes the photo sketches (problem 2).

Same static, with and without the embedding · pick a test crash

Median over the 38 test crashes (pixel correlation between the two pictures; 1 = identical): version 1, with vs. without the embedding , while two different static seeds with the same embedding give . In version 1, the static decides the picture. In version 3 the numbers are and , so the embedding now changes the picture about as much as the static does.

Problem 2 · Look at the data at the size the model sees it

of the 288 sketches are drawn on top of an aerial photo. At full size they look fine. But our 64-pixel version measures darkness as ink, so they turn almost black. These all-black "sketches" taught versions 1 and 2 to fill the canvas with gray and dark blocks. Version 3 leaves them out (the cut: more than half the pixels inked; none of them are in the test set). Two more wide aerial sketches slipped under that cut: they become a dark band. A better rule is "more than 30% of pixels fully inked", which catches exactly 12.

Redrawing a test sketch from its own embedding · median rank of the true sketch (lower is better; chance 19.5)

Each fix helped. Version 3 is used on every other tab. The dashed reference (6.5) is not a model: it simply copies the training sketch whose embedding is closest. That copy still beats the decoder, a point we return to in the discussion.

Guidance: how hard to lean on the embedding · version 3, first 12 test crashes, same static

Without guidance (λ = 0) the true sketch's median rank is ; with λ = 2 it is . Guidance makes the outputs bolder and more specific to the embedding.

Going deeper (optional): classifier-free guidance
ε̃ = g(zt, w, t, ∅) + (1 + λ) · [ g(zt, w, t, cimg) − g(zt, w, t, ∅) ]

Because cimg was replaced by a learned "no embedding" vector ∅ on 10% of training examples, the same U-Net can guess the static with or without the embedding. The bracket is the part of the guess that comes from the embedding; λ > 0 exaggerates it. λ = 2 here equals guidance scale 3 in the unCLIP paper's notation (scale = 1 + λ). Ho and Salimans (2022), Classifier-free diffusion guidance.

Evaluation close

Baseline
No embedding at all (median rank ) and copying the training sketch nearest to the embedding (6.5). The decoder lands between them: 10.
Split and why it is honest
The decoder trained on train and validation sketches only. The 38 test sketches were never seen; only their embeddings were given at generation time.
Ugly cases
Outputs still have gray backgrounds and dark blocks; at 64 pixels all text labels and most lane markings are lost; two aerial sketches remain in training. The scorer judges overall layout through CLIP's eyes. It does not check whether the turning movement is right.

Step 3 · Bridge from the narrative's embedding to a sketch embedding

The decoder speaks cimg. For a new crash we only have the narrative, so only ctxt. Step 1 made the two point in similar directions, but they are not the same vector, and they sit in different regions (the modality gap from the unCLIP handout). The prior's job is to turn ctxt into a believable cimg. We compare four priors, all trained on the 207 training pairs, with settings chosen on validation.

Four ways to get a sketch embedding from a narrative · and the diffusion prior in detail

Why a diffusion prior: one narrative fits many sketches (the officer's drawing style, how much of the intersection is shown), so unCLIP samples a sketch embedding instead of predicting a single average one. P0 to P2 are the simple baselines it has to beat.

L = ‖ cimg − h(zt, t, ctxt) ‖²
zt
the matched cimg (scaled by √512) buried under step-t static
h
the prior transformer; its readout token is its guess of the clean cimg
ctxt
the narrative's embedding from step 1 (dropped 10% of the time, for guidance)
In words: the same denoising game as the decoder, played on 512 numbers instead of 4,096 pixels, with the narrative as the hint.

P3 training loss · batches of 64 pairs

P3 validation · mean rank of the true sketch embedding among 43

The step with the best validation rank () is kept. Guidance was chosen on validation too: λ = (validation mean rank ).

Where does each guess land? · median cosine to the nearest training-sketch embedding (test narratives)

The modality gap, measured: a real but unseen test sketch has a training sketch at cosine 0.57. The raw narrative embedding (P0) is at 0.33, outside the region of sketch embeddings that the decoder learned from. Every prior pulls the guess back in: ridge lands where real sketches land, the diffusion prior lands closer to training sketches than real new sketches do, and lookup lands exactly on one.

Results in embedding space (test, before any drawing)

Problem 3 · The diffusion prior learned no variety

Eight samples for the same narrative, each from different static, have a median cosine of to each other: the same answer every time. This is not a bug in the sampler. In the training data, every narrative has exactly one sketch, and with 207 narratives each easy to tell apart, the best denoiser can recognize the narrative and output its sketch embedding regardless of the static. It has no examples of "one narrative, several sketches" to learn variety from. The prior became a regression, and the "best of 2" step chooses between two identical guesses.

Evaluation close

Baseline
No prior (P0, median rank 14) and lookup (P2, 13). The diffusion prior (13.5) does not beat them; all four are within noise of each other and well short of a useful pairing.
Split and why it is honest
Trained on the 207 training pairs; ridge penalty, best step and guidance picked on the 43 validation pairs; test scored once.
Ugly cases
A prior cannot add information that ctxt lacks: it moves the guess into the sketch region, but toward a plausible sketch, not the right one. With one sketch per narrative, it cannot learn variety.

Put it together: narrative → prior → decoder → sketch

For each of the 38 test narratives: encode it (step 1), turn ctxt into a sketch-embedding guess (step 3), and let the decoder draw from that guess (step 2, version 3, two static seeds). Then score every output with the rank of the true sketch. The rows at the bottom of the chart are references that copy a real training sketch instead of drawing one.

How close is each output to the right sketch? · 38 test crashes × 2 seeds

Reading: every narrative-driven row (gold) sits at chance, as does the floor with no embedding. The decoder can draw from a sketch's own embedding (green), so the drawing step works to a degree. What fails is getting from the narrative to the right sketch embedding.

Six test crashes · the first two (by ID) of each of the three most common crash types, chosen before looking

Real sketches are not shown on this page; if you are enrolled, open each crash ID in the course dataset to compare. The decoder never saw these six sketches. The copy check below measures how close each kind of output is to its nearest training sketch.

Is the decoder just copying training sketches?

A copy of a training sketch would score 1.0. A real new test sketch has a training sketch at . Outputs driven by narratives () lean a little toward the training sketches, but they are not copies.

Evaluation close

Baseline
No embedding (17.5), and the reference rows that copy a training sketch picked by the narrative (19) or by the sketch's own embedding (6.5). Retrieval with the narrative is as poor as generation with it.
Split and why it is honest
Test narratives and sketches were never used to train or tune anything; corridors differ from training.
Ugly cases
Only 38 crashes and 2 seeds: differences of two or three ranks between rows are noise. The scorer looks at the overall layout at 64 pixels. A sketch with the right intersection but the wrong turning movement can still score well, and vice versa.

Explore the 38 test crashes

If you are enrolled, open the crash in your copy of the course dataset first: read its narrative, picture the sketch, then look at the real one. Then compare it with what each route produced. For each output, the rank of the true sketch is shown (1 = best of 38). What each route drew · 64 × 64, as the models see it

What this run teaches

  1. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. The three steps are trained separately, so each can look fine on its own while the chain fails. Here step 1 is the weak link: a narrative ranks its own sketch about 14th of 38. The prior cannot add information that ctxt does not carry, so every narrative-driven output lands at chance. Before training a generator, measure the pairing on held-out data. If retrieval is near chance, generation will be too.
  2. Check that the condition changes the output. Version 1 of the decoder had a falling loss and produced sketch-like pictures, yet it ignored the embedding. The cheap check is to keep the static fixed and swap the condition. If the picture barely changes, the condition is not being used. Also check the scale at which a condition enters a network: here 512 numbers of size about 0.04 were drowned out by the step signal.
  3. Look at the data at the size the model sees it. Twelve aerial-photo sketches turned into black squares or dark bands at 64 pixels. Nobody would notice them in the original files, and they taught the decoder to paint gray.
  4. Variety has to be in the data. unCLIP's diffusion prior can sample many sketch embeddings for one caption only because its training set had many images for similar captions. With one sketch per narrative and 207 narratives, it learned one answer per narrative.
  5. With little data, retrieval beats generation. Copying the training sketch nearest to the embedding (median rank 6.5) beats drawing from that embedding (10). With 240 sketches and an hour of CPU, a decoder cannot draw as well as a lookup can find. It is worth asking whether you need a new sketch or a similar real one.
  6. The modality gap is real, and a prior only fixes half of it. The raw narrative embedding sits outside the sketch region (cosine 0.33 to the nearest sketch vs. 0.57 for a real sketch). The priors move it inside, toward a plausible sketch rather than the right one.

What it would take to make this work

  • Many more pairs. CLIP learned its pairing from 400 million image–caption pairs; we had 207. State crash databases hold many years of long-form reports with both parts, so this is largely a data-access problem, not a modeling one.
  • Structured captions. Coded fields (crash type, each vehicle's maneuver, lanes, traffic control, intersection type) are short, consistent and exactly the facts a sketch must get right. They could serve as a second "caption" next to the narrative (unCLIP's prior also reads the caption's tokens, not only ctxt).
  • A sketch format that keeps geometry. A 64-pixel bitmap loses lane lines, labels and arrows. A vector sketch (road edges, vehicle boxes with headings, movement arrows) is smaller and keeps exactly what an engineer checks. Diffusion can be trained on such lists of shapes and paths just as well as on pixels.
  • An evaluation an engineer would trust. CLIP similarity rewards the overall look. A checklist scored by a person or a parser (right intersection type? right turning vehicle? right directions?) measures what a crash reviewer cares about.
  • Compute. Everything here ran on 2 CPU cores. A GPU would allow a larger decoder, longer training and 128- or 256-pixel sketches.

When to keep the classical method

If the goal is a draft sketch for a report, a template filled from the coded fields (intersection type, vehicle maneuvers and directions) is exact, explainable and needs no training data. If the goal is a realistic example, retrieving a similar real sketch beats generating one at this data size. A generator earns its place only when you need many new, plausible variations, for example to test a sketch-reading model, and when you have enough pairs to learn the pairing well.

Fit card and check yourself

Fit card — the unCLIP recipe (pair → decoder → prior) on paired transportation data

Idea in one sentence
Learn a shared embedding for two views of the same event, learn to redraw one view from its own embedding, then learn a bridge from the other view's embedding, so that one view can generate the other.
Why it works (the logic)
Splitting the job lets the hardest part, drawing, learn from every example of that view, paired or not. Only the pairing and the bridge need matched pairs. Diffusion is the training method for the decoder and the prior, not a network architecture.
Fits these tasks
Drafting the missing view, finding the matching view, flagging pairs that disagree. Leverage labels: generation · retrieval.
Needs this data
Matched pairs for steps 1 and 3 (207 was far too few; think thousands at least), as many examples as possible of the view you generate for step 2, and no hand labels.
Breaks when
The pairing is weak, since every later step inherits it; the embedding drops a detail that matters (which vehicle turned, which way); the data hold one picture per description, so the prior cannot learn variety; the data look different at the model's resolution.
Keep the classical method when
A template can draw the picture from coded fields, a similar real example is good enough, or the output must be exact (a legal record) rather than plausible.

Check yourself

  1. An agency has 20,000 scanned crash sketches but only 300 typed narratives. Which of the three steps can use all 20,000 sketches, and which are limited to 300? Where would you expect the weakest link, and what would you measure first to find out?
    HintThe decoder on this page trained on sketches alone. Steps 1 and 3 need pairs. Measure held-out pairing rank against chance before training anything else.
  2. A classmate shows you a conditional diffusion model whose outputs look sharp and realistic. Name two quick checks from this page that tell you whether the outputs actually depend on the condition, and say what result would worry you.
    HintSame static with and without the condition (decoder tab). Compare with simply copying the nearest training example (pipeline tab).
  3. The diffusion prior here gives the same sketch embedding every time for the same narrative. Is that a bug? What would the training data need to contain for it to produce variety, and would that variety be useful for crash sketches?
    HintThink about how many sketches exist per narrative, and whether a reviewer wants many sketches or the right one.
  4. Your project pairs dashcam frames with the vehicle's CAN signals, and you want to generate frames for a rare maneuver. How would you split the data so the test is honest, and what number from step 1 would make you stop before training a decoder?
    HintSplit by route or by driver, as this page split by corridor. Stop if held-out retrieval is near chance (here, median rank 14 of 38 vs. chance 19.5 was already a warning).
  5. A reviewer says: "Your pipeline is at chance, so diffusion does not work for crash sketches." Using the decoder results, write two sentences that correct this conclusion without overselling it.
    HintSeparate the drawing step (median rank 10 from the sketch's own embedding) from the pairing step (14 in embedding space), and mention the retrieval reference (6.5).

Reproduce

Code, results and a README are in the class folder under genmodels/unclip_crash/. The scripts read your own copy of the course crash dataset. No data is stored with the code, and the dataset's terms of use apply.

python -I cu_prepare.py DATA_DIR WORK          # 64-px sketches + frozen CLIP features         (~3 min)
python -I cu_pairing_lit.py WORK               # step 1 (image side locked, text head)          (<1 min)
python -I cu_pairing.py WORK                   # step 1 with heads on both sides (comparison)   (<1 min)
python -I cu_text_features.py WORK             # side test: CLIP text vs word counts            (~1 min)
python -I cu_prior.py WORK                     # step 3: four priors                            (~10 min)
python -I cu_decoder.py WORK 6000 --no-photo   # step 2: decoder version 3 (resumable)          (~64 min)
python -I cu_generate.py WORK WORK/out/cu_decoder_6000.pt   # full pipeline, 38 test crashes    (~25 min)
python -I cu_companion_data.py WORK            # numbers and pictures for this page (re-checked)
python -I build_companion.py WORK              # writes this page

Data: the CGN 6933 course crash dataset (de-identified Florida long-form crash reports), shared with enrolled students only. This page shows model outputs and summary numbers, not the data: every sketch on it was drawn by the models.
